This paper explores the properties of an extended class of Lemaître-Tolman-Bondi spacetimes, denoted as $ltb^{(n,m)}_{a,b}$, where $a,b>0$ and $n,m\in \mathbb{N}$. The research reveals that the spacetimes in this class can be mapped to a subset of Bianchi cosmological models, specifically those of type $V_{n,m}^m$. The study examines the structure of these spacetimes, discusses their evolution, and examines the stability of their singularities. The findings demonstrate that the generalized LTB spacetimes exhibit distinct properties that set them apart from standard LTB models. The comparison highlights the diversity of LTB-like spacetimes, challenging the common misconception that all LTB models share identical characteristics. The research also raises questions about the applicability of the generalized LTB spacetimes in the context of dark matter phenomena, offering a new class of models for consideration.

A collection of quantum states with a specific level of nonlinearity, known as strongly nonlocal multipartite orthogonal sets, exhibits properties similar to discrete quantum phases, yet remains unexplored. This paper delves into the theory by defining this set and conducting an initial analysis. It also identifies the most non-orthogonal state within this set. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that measuring the non-orthogonality of these sets can be achieved by implementing a quantum experiment on entangled photons. The potential applications of these sets in quantum information theory are also discussed.

In the context of web user behavior, specific actions like visits are often taken by users within a certain timeframe. For instance, news websites frequently update their content every hour. Users may choose to bookmark the website to stay informed about the latest developments. While visit intentions provide valuable insights into users' goals, they are often overlooked in favor of focusing on actions such as clicks and impressions. In this paper, we explore the idea of incorporating visit intentions into online advertising optimization by developing a probabilistic model based on user and content characteristics. Our approach enables the identification of visit intentions for both news and e-commerce websites, where we implemented a probabilistic model to predict user visits. The results show that our model can predict the likelihood of visits within an hour with an average accuracy of 77% for news websites and 71% for e-commerce websites.

A reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) with transmissive capabilities can effectively transmit information by adjusting the phase shifts of its elements, thus generating a signal that moves within the receiver's space. This study explores the potential of an RIS-assisted communication system, taking into account both information transmission and channel monitoring. An optimization problem is developed to maximize the system's information transmission rate, while also utilizing channel state information (CSI) from pilot signals to estimate the channel and optimize the phase shifts. A high precision channel model is developed, allowing the system to achieve optimal transmission. Numerical results show that the system significantly outperforms existing technology when fully utilizing its available resources, thus solidifying its position as a key technology for future wireless communications.

Offline reinforcement learning seeks to develop optimal policies using pre-collected datasets without real-world interactions. Existing methods typically rely on maximizing expected returns or obtaining a policy's mean and variance. However, this approach has limitations, as it neglects the risk aspect, leading to potentially poor policy performance. To address this, we propose a risk-sensitive offline reinforcement learning method that enables learning with suboptimal data. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that our algorithm can converge quickly to a well-defined optimal policy, even under risk-sensitive conditions. Experimental results confirm that our method outperforms existing approaches on standard benchmarks.

We demonstrate how polymorphic functions in Haskell have implicit connections to specific types, known as free theorems. To illustrate this concept, we use examples to explain the idea and show how the application of a polymorphic function to various types can be seen as a universal interface. Furthermore, we explore how this notion can be applied to monads within Haskell and observe the implications it has on understanding monads more broadly.

Our research has identified a newly discovered galaxy located 7.5 million parsecs away, known as J0437+2456. With an observed redshift of z = 0.2006, this galaxy is classified as a typical galaxy for its age and is estimated to be approximately 1.1 billion parsecs away. Based on our findings, we have calculated the galaxy's mass to be approximately 11 times that of our sun, with a star mass range of 0.1 to 10 times that of our sun. The galaxy consists of a supermassive black hole, a pair of active nuclei, and is surrounded by a ring of dust and a long tail of gas extending 100 kiloparsecs into space. The galaxy is estimated to be approximately 130 million years old and is in its final stages of evolution. Our research suggests that the galaxy is in its final stages of evolution, with the supermassive black hole and one of the pair of active nuclei merging in the distant future.

This paper investigates configurations in the planar Newtonian three-body problem where the bodies or their velocities align, also known as generalised syzygies. Previous research has identified specific cases of collinear three-body syzygies. We expand on this knowledge by providing a comprehensive classification system that outlines all possible collinear and non-collinear syzygies for the three-body system. Additionally, our work outlines conditions under which certain configurations can occur within the three-body problem. We also demonstrate the uniqueness of a particular type of three-body collinear syzygy under certain initial conditions. We employ numerical methods to verify the non-occurrence of non-collinear syzygies in the three-body system under certain closed three-body orbit conditions.

Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) measures the duration that fluorescent molecules emit light after being excited by a specific wavelength of light. FLIM offers the advantage of obtaining detailed information about the physical and chemical properties of a specimen through a parameter that is not available through conventional imaging methods. However, accurately determining the lifetime of fluorescent molecules is challenging due to several factors, including the presence of background interference and decay caused by the excitation source. To address these issues, we have developed an innovative technique that utilizes deep learning to enhance FLIM images. We have also created a synthetic dataset that mimics real-life FLIM data through a mathematical model. Using this dataset, we have trained a generative adversarial network to generate high-quality FLIM images. Furthermore, we have designed a Convolutional Neural Network to reconstruct the decay curve of fluorescent materials. The performance of both methods was evaluated through a series of experiments involving both simulated and real-life FLIM images. The results of these experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality FLIM images.

Personalized product search relies heavily on accurate user preference modeling.  Recent advancements in attention-based methods have led to significant improvements in user embeddings and product summaries; however, these methods neglect to incorporate product descriptions and category information, which are crucial for effective user preferences.  Moreover, user-product interactions vary depending on individual search sessions, making it essential to model session-level interactions that adapt dynamically.  To address these challenges, we introduce a new session-dependent attention mechanism (SDA) that simultaneously learns user preferences at both item and session levels.  In contrast to traditional attention methods, our approach is more efficient and scalable due to its use of a single-vector attention vector that eliminates the need for additional weights.  Experimental results on a real-world e-commerce dataset demonstrate that SDA outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a relative gain of 2.47% in terms of NDC and a 4.13% gain in terms of overall revenue compared to the best baseline method.

Our research introduces a novel approach to graph embedding using a combination of variational inference and energy-based models. By learning an energy function for a dynamic sequence of latent spaces, our method aims to produce a stable and consistent set of representations. We achieve this through a novel variational recurrent network that balances the influence of previous representations in the process of generating the next one. By employing a novel metric that measures representation similarity, our method can effectively maintain consistency across the sequence. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in a variety of applications, including link prediction and node classification, and evaluate its performance on real-world datasets, showcasing its superior generalization capability compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access enables high spectral efficiency while minimizing signaling overhead. However, it poses significant detection and estimation challenges for the base station. This paper presents a new approach, called the multi-layer orthogonal omni-power maximum likelihood detector, designed to quickly and efficiently decode grant-free signals with square-root relationship between layers. By simultaneously detecting signals from multiple users, this approach significantly outperforms traditional methods that focus on individual users. To validate its performance, the paper includes both theoretical and numerical results, including a comparison with a more complex detector based on tree structures.

Compressed sensing explores algorithms to retrieve a sparse signal or code from low-level measurements. Identifying a suitable sparse coding matrix in this context is crucial and has received significant research attention. Recent breakthroughs have revealed that the sparse coding matrix can be chosen randomly from a Gaussian distribution, leading to nearly optimal recovery of sparse signals. Building upon this discovery, our study presents a unified framework that applies random matrix theory to derive near-optimal recovery outcomes for both sparse and low-rank matrix reconstruction. Specifically, we leverage the theory of random matrices to analyze the performance of matrix recovery using both the basis pursuit and L1-regularized least squares methods on matrices.

Deep neural network training can be significantly improved by incorporating data augmentation techniques. Recent research has demonstrated that a particular type of augmentation, based on transformation of a neural network's latent space, can be particularly effective. Notably, this approach allows for the creation of diverse samples through various operations such as rotation, flipping, and brightness changes. We have developed an innovative, trainable method to generate synthetic training images for enhanced accuracy in domain adaptation and improved generalization. Notably, this approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing neural networks without requiring modification to the model architecture or hyperparameters. We have tested our proposed method on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN datasets and observed improved performance compared to a widely used state-of-the-art method.

This paper demonstrates that for certain types of mathematical structures known as Jordan rings of self-adjoint matrices, derived from the algebraic principles of self-adjoint 2x2 matrices, any operation based on the rules of inner derivation, specifically those applicable to 2-local operations within this framework, can be expressed as a combination of a specific inner derivation and a non-commutative operation.

We've developed a comprehensive mathematical framework to analyze the behavior of closed paths in systems governed by time-dependent parameters, drawing inspiration from Berry's phase in adiabatic quantum systems. This framework involves a generalized parameter that governs the rate of change in parameters, enabling us to derive a precise formula for a parameterized version of Berry's phase. We've also extended this formula to complex cases where parameters change both slowly and rapidly, and numerically compared our results with exact simulations of quantum circuits to verify their accuracy. This work has implications for designing and optimizing adiabatic quantum computing algorithms.

We demonstrate the existence of compacton matter waves in a binary mixture of Bose-Einstein condensates, examining their stability as well. Our investigation reveals that the outcome of the phase transition from modulational instability to compacton formation is heavily influenced by the interplay between the two key parameters - the cross coupling coefficient and the relative population of the two BECs. Under certain parameter constraints, compactons emerge within a specific, bounded area on the parameter space. Interestingly, our stability analysis reveals that compactons are generally unstable, but their fragility is determined by the parameter values. A longer wavelength of compactons tends to make them more stable, while their fragility increases with larger amplitudes. Our results also show that the monostable and bistable regimes can be achieved in this system, offering potential for experimental verification and further exploration of compacton formation in multi-component BEC systems.

The heavy-quark spin symmetry (HQSS) is assumed to organize the properties of the newly identified baryons $\Xi_{cc}(\3620)$, $\Xi_{cc}^+(3920)$, $\Theta_c(3090)$ and $\Theta_c(3150)$. Their masses are predicted, and existing data for other particles are used to confirm these predictions. We also present a proposal for detecting these predicted baryons through experiments that involve the transfer of a $\pi$ meson.

This paper investigates a specific type of non-local operator known as the non-local fractional Laplace operator on graphs or metric spaces with particular properties. The main objective is to demonstrate the existence of smooth approximations for this operator's action on bounded functions in various geometric settings. The research also involves establishing a fundamental inequality for a particular class of fractional Laplace operators on Riemannian manifolds.

We're investigating a specific type of particle called the axion-like particle, ALP, which interacts with Standard Model bosons in a particular way. We've found that when ALPs are produced in the early universe and then interact with a gravitational lens, it can create multiple images, allowing for a new method to search for ALPs. By studying the gravitational lensing effect, we've calculated the ALP flux that can be measured by the Chandra telescope, which could help us set tighter constraints on the ALP sector.

In recent years, the development of specialized accelerators has been directed towards specific application domains, such as machine learning and deep learning, leading to a notable increase in processing speed. However, this has resulted in a lack of focus on general-purpose processors, causing them to become less efficient and capable. In response, this research proposes a new cooperative technique that enables general-purpose processors to collaborate with other processors, in this case, FPGAs, to significantly enhance performance and energy efficiency. By utilizing a new hardware abstraction layer and a new co-design framework, this technique allows applications to work seamlessly with the FPGA, resulting in a substantial 5.8-68x speedup and 3-65% improvement in energy efficiency and system performance, respectively.

Deep learning algorithms have achieved remarkable success in computer vision tasks. Pre-trained deep networks can now be leveraged for various downstream applications via conversion to the floating-point format, utilizing large datasets for training. Nonetheless, direct hardware execution of these models is often restricted by their resource-intensive nature. To overcome this limitation, this paper presents a novel method for accelerating neural network execution on FPGAs, particularly suitable for applications involving diverse models with known input sizes. The proposed approach relies on the generation of efficient path-mapping lookup tables, input and output data buffering, and optimized processing pipelines, all of which are designed to optimize performance, area, and latency. Furthermore, these components can be easily integrated into a hierarchical structure to accommodate multiple models with distinct input sizes. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving substantial performance gains, with latency reductions of up to 2.5x and significant improvements in area complexity compared to existing state-of-the-art FPGA implementations.

The presence of a locally Lipschitz variable leads to the singular nature of the quasi-linear elliptic system under consideration. However, the use of a previously established definition allows for the reformulation of this system into a standard quasi-linear elliptic system, for which the existence of a solution can be confirmed using well-known methods.

Recurrent neural networks are particularly effective in learning complex patterns across extensive time periods, but training them for long-term tasks is notoriously difficult and often requires significant amounts of fine-tuning. To overcome this, we developed a new training method that involves integrating a secondary network that utilizes a self-attention mechanism to focus on specific segments of the network's entire sequence data. This secondary network serves as an additional memory or attention mechanism that can be used to improve the network's performance on tasks involving long-term sequences. We demonstrate the potential of our approach in significantly enhancing the network's ability to learn from long-term sequences on a variety of complex tasks such as modeling the distribution of random walks and identifying language patterns in long-term contexts.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking algorithm for creating policies in large, stochastic systems that can adapt and learn, using a type of neural network called a policy network. We leverage the concept of large deviations to approximate the optimal solution of complex system problems, then use it to create a target function for our policy network to minimize. Our method is flexible and can be applied to various Markov Decision Processes and linear-quadratic systems. Moreover, our policy guarantees a stable system operation, and our training method ensures that the policy is indeed an optimal solution to the original problem. We also demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through numerical experiments on a high-dimensional stock trading problem, showing its superior performance over other existing methods.

A novel technique for accelerating electrons using a self-interfering electron beam is introduced, producing an attosecond electron bunch with high energy and angular alignment. Analytical models were developed to investigate the dynamics of electron self-interference, yielding a general equation for the evolving phase error over time. By adjusting the electron beam's spatial distribution, it is possible to achieve a perfect circular orbit and mitigate the effects of space-charge effects on the electron beam's phase error. Numerical simulations were conducted on an existing facility to verify the model's accuracy and demonstrate the production of a high-energy attosecond electron bunch. This technique has the potential to be used in next-generation accelerators and radiation sources.

Key human experiences like creativity, self-awareness, and decision-making have long been enigmatic, particularly when it comes to measuring and defining them. However, recent theories have linked these phenomena to a fundamental scalar field, with its units being a measure of the complexity of life forms, suggesting it's a universal indicator of life's vital force. This vital force is said to increase as organisms progress from inorganic to living, and ultimately, as they progress from simple to complex. This research aims to demonstrate that the human experience of creativity, self-awareness, and decision-making can be seen as manifestations of this scalar field, leading to increased complexity. This is achieved through the development of a geometric model that maps these human experiences to geometric shapes, with each dimension representing a corresponding aspect of the field. This model allows us to explore the underlying dynamics of our human experience and our inherent drive for complexity.

To ensure effective policy-making for Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI), reliable and accurate information is crucial. Open access policies such as the European Open Access Agreement aim to address this challenge by making research outputs available to everyone. Despite this, the extent to which institutions comply with these policies remains unclear. This study investigates the extent to which European universities adhere to open access requirements during the 2020 publication year. We analyzed a comprehensive dataset of 2020 DOAJ publications from 206 institutions, which yielded promising results. Our findings indicate that a majority of these universities adhere to the conditions set by the PLoS, with 62% of their publications meeting this standard. Moreover, our study shows that a significant number of institutions have made substantial progress towards achieving this goal, with 51 institutions improving their compliance rate compared to the previous year. Our results suggest that a combination of internal and external factors, including the presence of open access policies and institutional support, contributes to the success of these efforts. This study demonstrates that public access to university publications has a significant impact on the development of evidence-based policy-making for STI systems, ultimately contributing to the creation of a global open access network.

The primary focus of smartphone security has traditionally been on preventing direct attacks on devices, while side-channel vulnerabilities, which can compromise data confidentiality through indirect channels, have gained significant attention in recent years. These vulnerabilities, which can exploit sensitive information leaked through various channels, have become a major concern in the security community. The increasing number of side-channel vulnerabilities discovered every year highlights the need for effective security measures to protect smartphone users. This thesis aims to address this need by developing practical security techniques to protect against side-channel attacks that exploit cache-based and memory-side channels. The first contribution of this thesis is the development of a novel cache-based leakage detection and mitigation technique that uses a unique combination of basic cache operations. The second contribution is the development of a set of high-performance and efficient mitigation techniques that can be used in conjunction with the detection technique to protect against side-channel attacks. The third contribution is the development of a novel countermeasure that utilizes a unique hardware component to protect against side-channel attacks. The effectiveness of these techniques is demonstrated through a series of experiments that show a significant reduction in side-channel vulnerabilities and the impact of these vulnerabilities on real-world systems. The results of this investigation also highlight the potential of these techniques in protecting against side-channel attacks in real-world scenarios.

Ethereum's decentralized applications (dApps) have become increasingly popular, with the majority of them utilizing the Ethereum blockchain for secure transactions and smart contracts since its inception in 2017. Analyzing Ethereum's transaction data can help understand the underlying interactions between dApps, their users, and the Ethereum ecosystem as a whole. This study examines the Ethereum blockchain for network characteristics using transaction data from 2017 to 2021 and presents a comprehensive analysis of various network architectures. By identifying and comparing different types of Ethereum accounts based on their transaction patterns, the research uncovers unique relationships between accounts, including those between Ethereum accounts and external addresses. This distinction enables the development of a framework to categorize accounts into distinct types, with the results showing that the majority (80.7%) fall into one category, while specific account types have distinct features. The research findings can be applied to dApp development, particularly in anti-money laundering and anti-mandatory laws, to identify and categorize user accounts.

Our study of the LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ (LAO/STO) interface in a 2D electron system reveals that the system's resistance is significantly influenced by the amount of light it receives, with the effect being much greater than what is typical for a material like copper. When exposed to bright light, the resistance decreases by as much as 50% within 30 seconds, only to slowly increase back up over the course of several hours in the absence of additional excitation. This significant increase in resistance when exposed to light indicates a transfer of charge between the material's layers, with the effect being reversible and influenced by the amount of light it receives. Further investigation using Hall effect measurements found that the change in resistance is caused by an increase in carrier concentration and, to a lesser degree, a decrease in mobility of charge carriers.

A novel bunched logic, referred to as BV, is introduced by merging Boolean and subformula junctional logic with positive and negative modalities. This logic incorporates a diverse set of connectives, including Boolean operators, an implication, and three modal operators, namely positive modalities ($\forall$), negative modalities ($!$), and modal implication ($\Deduce$), along with various modal operators, including modal conjunction ($*$), disjunction ($\S$), and disjunction of modal subformulae ($\S$). The logic, in its full version, is characterized by a complex decision problem, however various abstractions are proposed to make it more manageable. The paper demonstrates that a particular version of BV, referred to as the reduced bunched logic, is decidable and is capable of encoding the $\lambda_{\mu,2}$ calculus. This result is proven by establishing a fundamental reduction from the problem of provability in reduced BV to $\mu$-calculus.
The pentagon identity for quantum dilogarithms and the five-term relation in MacLane's surgery exact sequence are demonstrated to be essentially equivalent.

We have developed a machine learning model that can estimate the photometric redshifts of galaxies in terms of their physical observables. Our model uses the data from the VHS survey, which includes galaxy images taken in five different filters and redshift information obtained from spectroscopy. We first converted the redshift information into physical ages and metallic compositions for the galaxies, using a simplified cosmological model. We then trained a regression model to map the photometric data to these physical observables. Our model's performance was evaluated by comparing its predictions to independent measurements of physical ages and metallic compositions. Our results show that our model's performance was comparable to that of existing methods that used spectroscopic redshifts. We also found that our model's predictions were consistent with the uncertainties associated with the measured redshifts.

Complex computer models in various fields like engineering and medicine can be effectively analyzed using Gaussian Process emulators, which approximate expensive functions with a more affordable surrogate. However, these emulators' accuracy can be compromised by the data used to train them, particularly when certain input parameters are not well-represented. In such cases, the emulator's validity is questionable, and determining its reliability is a pressing challenge. This research focuses on a specific issue: providing reliable error estimates for emulated predictions when certain areas of the input parameter space are not adequately covered. By examining the accuracy of the Gaussian Process emulator in the log-likelihood sense, we establish a connection between the estimated error and the parameter posterior distribution. This relationship is expressed as a mathematical inequality, providing a more precise error bound than current existing methods. This error bound is particularly insightful when dealing with posterior distributions that exhibit a local maximum. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the error bound is tightly bounded by the parameter standard deviation in certain cases, offering a more accurate error estimate than current methods.

We examine the QC-DMRG method's performance using the Heisenberg Hamiltonian on a 2D square lattice, focusing on two-electron systems. Our results show that for such systems, the optimal bond dimension is indeed infinite, but we find that a bond dimension of 24 is sufficient for accurate calculations. Additionally, we clarify the need for supplementary strong orbitals in the algorithm and specify the method's optimal parameters.

To address the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental predictions of the muon anomalous magnetic moment, we propose an extension of the Standard Model that includes an additional $SU(2)_X$ gauge factor with higgs fields. This new framework enables the muon anomalous magnetic moment to be aligned with experimental findings. Furthermore, the model yields testable particle physics predictions, such as a doublet lepton sector in the electroweak scale and observable signals for the new $SU(2)_X$ gauge boson at upcoming particle colliders like the LHC and the future $e^+e^-$ colliders.

To mitigate the growing maintenance demands of intricate high-resolution coastal and ocean models, a potential solution lies in developing machine learning-based surrogates. A key challenge in this area is identifying the most suitable machine learning methods for this application. A novel comparison framework is introduced that allows for a systematic evaluation of various machine learning approaches. A set of basic techniques including decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting are applied to a dynamic ocean model, and their performance is assessed in predicting velocity, temperature, and salinity levels. The methods are evaluated using a range of metrics, including those focused on statistical aspects and geometric proximity. The results indicate that decision trees can serve as a good starting point for future investigations, and random forests demonstrate promising potential.

In an effort to increase transparency and reproducibility, we are releasing a comprehensive CMB analysis toolset, allowing researchers to recreate our pipeline for the Bicep/Keck 2010 data using the original software components as they existed then. This open-source package, LKHM v1.0, is built with Python 2.7, Python packages, and CUDA 4.0/5.0 that are all downloadable from public repositories. By releasing our code, we aim to accelerate the growth of the computational physics community, foster accountability for open science initiatives, and promote the use of reproducible research.

We explore a simplified model of Turing instability in an odorant reaction-diffusion system within a neuron model, focusing on the conditions under which Turing instability occurs and examining the collective behavior of neurons in a one-dimensional spatial arrangement with periodic boundary conditions in terms of their temporal dynamics and stability boundaries.

We analyze the implications of introducing a "phantom" deformation to pure Yang-Mills theory, where the gauge field's action is modified by a negative energy component. This modification gives rise to a new energy scale. Our findings indicate that the quantum corrections to this modified theory are unexpectedly eliminated due to cancellation, thereby preserving the non-renormalization properties of the gauge field's propagator. Furthermore, the modified theory's spectrum of vacua is investigated and shown to be distinct from the spectrum of vacua present in quantum chromodynamics (QCD).

Our research examines the polarization properties of photoluminescence in GaAs/AlGaAs single-heterostructure nanowires using polarization microscopy and micro-photoluminescence.  The study focuses on a specific nanowire with a 0.3 $\mu$m wide core, which exhibits an unusual radial polarization effect.  The polarization analysis of the nanowire's radial and longitudinal components at 77 K under in-plane and transverse excitation revealed a polarization degree of 0.9.  The study further investigates the polarization of the band edge emission and its transition to the valence band transition by varying the laser wavelength.  The findings suggest that the valence band transition's radial polarization effect diminishes as the laser energy approaches the band edge emission transition.

Inferring an opponent's priorities in negotiations through social interaction is known as opponent modeling. This technique is crucial in negotiations involving one-on-one interactions where the goal is to align one's offers with the opponent's hidden preferences, ultimately increasing the chance of a successful negotiation. To achieve this, we propose using language as a key source of information to infer these priorities and developed a language-aware neural network model that learns to identify the relative importance of negotiation objectives in one-on-on negotiations. Our model is trained to predict the negotiation objectives' importance from the conversation history and we tested it on a negotiation dataset with successful and failed negotiations provided with the dialogue transcripts. Our results show that this model can accurately infer the negotiation objectives' importance and achieve a significant classification accuracy.

In a braneworld setting, we investigate the impact of dynamical string tension on a string's movement. The string tension is a function of both boundary and edge variables. We derive the equations of motion for a Nambu-Goto string, which is situated in the radially symmetric space of a braneworld with a specific type of curvature. We establish that in this context, the string can remain confined to a specific location on the boundary, and that the presence of dynamical string tension naturally prevents string movements away from this boundary.

Researchers and scholars have long recognized the value of experimentation for companies and policymakers, enabling precise causality assessments that inform decision-making despite limited budget constraints. To address the challenge of limited experimental budgets, scholars have developed the concept of "matching" - a method for creating balanced, representative experimental groups. Although previous matching methods focused on static, budget-unlimited settings, this paper extends the idea to online, cost-sensitive settings, introducing an efficient, representative matching technique that employs stratified random sampling to minimize group imbalances and optimize sample size allocation, thus maximizing the efficiency of online field experiments.

The atomic arrangement of the (001)-gamma-Al2O3/(001)-silicon crystal interface was determined through ab initio simulations, which revealed that the interface is composed of four distinct layers of atoms with no vacancies or additional inclusions. Silicon atoms at the interface within the interface region are surrounded by four oxygen atoms from aluminium oxide molecules, while the outer layers of silicon atoms have a three-atom arrangement. Each aluminium and four silicon atoms within the interface are bonded with one oxygen atom, with three additional silicon atoms and one oxygen atom forming a unique configuration. The interface is composed of alternating layers of atoms with four atoms per layer and one atom per layer, with a total of six layers of atoms, which exhibits an anisotropic and asymmetrical structure. The interface is also found to be highly reactive, with a significant increase in the charge density at the interface, which facilitates the interaction between the interface and surrounding atoms. The interface is also found to be highly reactive towards diatomic molecules, which can bind to the interface via a shared pair of atoms, with a significant charge density increase, while the interface can also accommodate up to one molecule per unit cell without causing a jump in the interface structure.

This research explores the application of non-linear equations of state (NL EoS) to simulate the behavior of Black Holes in four-dimensional scenarios where axions and dilatons interact. Employing a quadratic model of NL EoS, the study aims to model the physical properties of these Black Holes within the axion-dilaton system. To achieve this, it assesses how the results are affected by the application of different forms of NL EoS parameters. By analyzing the impact of these variations, the study seeks to establish a comprehensive framework for modeling these Black Holes. To accomplish this, the researchers utilize various analytical and numerical methods to estimate the functions in question. The outcomes of these methods are then compared to one another. The study also examines the behavior of these Black Holes through both numerical integration and graphical representation. The outcomes of this analysis reveal that the proposed NL EoS model is capable of accurately modeling Black Holes.

Between 1977 and 2009, the shipping industry underwent a significant transformation, resulting in a substantial decline in freight rates, the collapse of numerous shipping companies, and widespread job losses. This period, known as the container crisis, had a profound impact on the industry and the local community in South Shields, where the shipping company George W. Waterhouse and Sons played a significant role. The company was faced with intense competition, poor freight rates, and struggles to pay off its debts. An examination of historical records, including diaries, letters, and newspaper articles, provides valuable insights into the difficulties the company faced during this period. The personal accounts of James Green, a young apprentice at the time, are particularly significant, as they reveal the challenges and difficulties he encountered both at sea and in business. Waterhouse and Sons ultimately survived the crisis, making it a testament to the company's resilience and ability to learn from its mistakes.

Real-time data analysis applications, such as security systems and data monitoring services, heavily rely on efficient and accurate anomaly detection systems. These systems must be able to process a high volume of data in real-time, detecting anomalies both consistently and effectively. The performance of these detectors is influenced by several factors including data distribution, available feature sets, and the ability to handle non-stationary data. A new method, called FPD, has been developed to improve the accuracy of streaming data anomaly detection. FPD leverages a feature selection approach to identify the most relevant features and applies a statistical-based ensemble method to account for non-stationary data. The results of experiments conducted on established datasets show that FPD achieves high accuracy with minimal features, and outperforms existing methods in terms of detection precision.

Accurate segmentation of gliomas is crucial for developing effective treatment plans and improving outcomes for patients. Conventional methods rely on machine learning algorithms that use imaging features to classify tumors, but they often struggle with varying tumor sizes, shapes, and locations. To address this issue, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes a transformer model to enhance the classification of tumors. By incorporating spatial relationships between tumor substructures, our approach has significantly improved the accuracy of segmentation. We have identified the key substructures of gliomas that are critical for classification, including the enhancing part, non-enhancing core, and T2 fluid. To further refine our approach, we have incorporated a multi-scale feature fusion technique that leverages the strengths of both local and global features. By using a patch-based attention mechanism, our approach has improved the accuracy of segmentation and achieved superior performance on the multi-scale feature fusion task. The results of our study demonstrate that our approach has achieved a mean Dice score of 0.84, significantly outperforming other methods.

A hypothetical particle called the triplon, which exists in certain types of spin systems with global Ising-invariance, has been of great interest to researchers. To investigate the properties of triplons, researchers have been using a specific mathematical model known as the quantum random phase approximation. However, this model has a significant flaw, which causes it to provide inaccurate predictions for certain types of spin systems. To overcome this problem, we have developed a new approach that improves the quantum random phase approximation. By incorporating a new method that takes into account the effects of certain types of spin interactions, we have been able to accurately calculate key properties of spin systems, including their energy levels and patterns of spin arrangement. Furthermore, our approach has allowed us to accurately describe the behavior of spin systems over time, including their patterns of spin arrangement and the way that these systems lose energy over time.

This article introduces a convergence criterion, statistical convergence via asymptotic density, and expands existing work on the subject. The study includes a sequence of fractional monotone functions, ultimately leading to a finding on the convergence of a specific type of integral in relation to the sequence's behavior.

This paper aims to derive the optimal error bound in the computer simulation of a specific nonlinear wave equation. Utilizing a novel numerical method, a finite difference scheme is developed and its efficiency is rigorously analyzed using functional analysis techniques. The resulting proof of the error estimate is completely independent of any small parameters present in the equation.

This paper explores the wellposedness of a highly nonlinear parabolic system, 
involving a state variable u and an artifact variable v, influenced by a nonlinear function g. 
This function g is based on the solution's pair (u,v) and is defined within a Hilbert space framework. 
Key to the wellposedness proof is a modified version of the Babuska-Brezzi Theorem. 
Additionally, a stable finite element method is developed to approximate the solution, 
resulting in a semidiscrete problem that maintains the system's coercivity and continuity properties. 
A fully discrete version of the problem is then established using a space-discrete finite element method, 
yielding a strong convergence scheme for the fully discrete solution, 
with error estimates matched by numerical experiments.

In a system of closely packed, charged quantum layers, a specific type of exciton called charged interlayer excitons (IELs) can be created, which have significant implications for both quantum science and physics. IELs exhibit unique properties when exposed to a magnetic field perpendicular to the layers. Our study delves into the fundamental physics of IELs by employing a numerical method to solve the Dirac equation under the influence of Coulomb interaction and magnetic fields. Our findings indicate that IELs display an unusual spin polarization in response to the magnetic field. Our results also show that spin-polarized IELs can be produced in graphene layers, while those in van der Waals heterostructures formed with transition metals exhibit a magnetic field threshold for spin-polarization that is relatively low.

The radial velocity precision of 0.1 km/s is achieved using a compact, robust astrophysical spectrograph equipped with a CCD camera and a micro-optics based spectrograph. A compact, two-inch diameter setup allows for efficient use of optical components, eliminating the need for complex optics and a telescope adapter tube. The spectrograph design incorporates a unique optical configuration featuring a 16x magnification, a 0.5-inch entrance, and a 2-inch diameter CCD camera. The compact astrophysical spectrograph offers a cost-effective solution for radial velocity measurements, requiring minimal maintenance and no complex optics.

A novel neural network architecture has been proposed for efficiently solving the inverse scattering problem using a forward scattering data input. The model's parameters are directly obtained without requiring a comparison with measured data, offering significant computational advantages over traditional optimization methods. The network's performance was demonstrated through its ability to accurately reconstruct permittivity models with varying levels of complexity, encompassing diverse permittivity values and dimensions. Notably, the entire process can be completed within approximately 1 second for 2D and up to 10 seconds for 3D data. The proposed approach exhibits superior performance and faster operational speeds compared to existing machine learning-based inversion methods.

Reliability engineering's accelerated degradation testing (ADT) has become a crucial tool for predicting product lifespan, despite recent studies providing conflicting conclusions on whether such models adequately capture the effects of increased stress on degradation paths. The existing literature on modeling ADT remains incomplete due to a lack of comprehensive models that accurately represent how degradation paths change when stress levels are elevated. This study develops a flexible Bayesian model for ADT using piecewise exponential distributions to represent degradation patterns and Gaussian process priors for the parameters' mean functions and scale parameters. The model's performance is evaluated using simulation studies and applied to a case study that models the degradation of Vibration Dampers in a Power Plant, providing posterior estimates and accounting for autocorrelation in the data.

We investigate the triangular flow $v_3$ and its connection to quark diffusion in Pb-Pb collisions at the relativistic energy of 2.76 TeV. Our analysis utilizes transport models, tested with global data, to understand $v_3$'s dependence on centrality and transverse momentum. The models, based on quark transport without a flow term, underpredict $v_3$ for small system sizes and high momenta. This discrepancy is resolved when a flow term is introduced, indicating initial momentum fluctuations are essential. Further analysis shows that quark diffusion primarily influences $v_3$ in small system sizes and high momenta. Our findings also suggest that within measured momentum ranges, quark diffusion's contribution to $v_3$ is comparable to that of initial triangularity fluctuations.

Observations by STEREO-A's suite of instruments revealed a unique, isothermal coherent radio signature associated with an interplanetary coronal mass ejection (ICME) that lacked a visible solar source. Due to its unusually low speed relative to the solar wind, this ICME was not visible from the perspective of the sun, prompting an investigation into its origin. Using data from STEREO-A, SOHO, Wind, and OEREC, we identified the origin of the isothermal emission source as an ICME that passed over STEREO-A at a time when it was in the process of becoming visible. This ICME had a low polytropic index, suggesting an isothermal thermodynamic behavior. This is consistent with the ICME's low speed in relation to other ICMEs observed by STEREO-A, which suggests that it may have been partially or wholly heated by magnetic reconnection. This is a common phenomenon in ICMEs observed by STEREO-A, and one that aligns with an alternative explanation for the isothermal radio signature - namely, that it results from magnetic reconnection at the ICME's front.

In the context of Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks utilizing the Random Waypoint Mobility Model, the mobility of nodes is represented as a measure-preserving transformation. Building on Birkhoff's pointwise ergodic theorem, we derive upper bounds for its consequences in terms of probability and time averages. Specifically, we demonstrate that the mobility of nodes, when considered as a system, is ergodic - with respect to a specific probability measure - and establish the stationarity of its velocity field. Additionally, we derive upper bounds for the maximum velocity reached by a single mobile station, as well as the minimum and maximum velocity of the entire group, along with their corresponding delays.

The production of $K^+K^-$ pairs has been extensively studied at the CERN Intersecting Storage Ring within a range of transverse momentum from 0.1 to 5 GeV/c and longitudinal momentum up to 6 GeV/c. The observed increase in the yield of $K^+K^-$ pairs at high longitudinal momentum was initially attributed to the Coulomb final state interaction, but this study reveals that the data also indicate a strong increase in the yield at low longitudinal momentum that cannot be explained solely by the Coulomb effect. This anomalous behavior can be accurately described by assuming the existence of a new strong interaction, akin to the strong interaction responsible for the production of mesons in the initial state.

Microscopic inertial masses related to different motion types in nuclear systems are calculated using time-dependent nuclear density functional theory, specifically with the Skyrme-Hartree-Fock method based on the Skyrme force. The method of collective inertial masses relies on the generator coordinate method, where a parameter related to collective motion is determined first. Collective micro-level masses are then determined by calculating matrix elements of inertial mass operators in a basis of generator coordinates, using a finite difference method to ensure convergence of these matrix elements. In this study, the Skyrme force is applied to calculate initial values of G-matrix elements for quadrupole and octupole collective motion, specifically in $^{20}$Ne and $^{16}$O isotopes. Calculations were performed for various Skyrme parametrizations and different cut-off values for the G-matrix, revealing that the calculated collective inertial masses are consistent with values obtained from collective models and density functional theory.

A significant challenge in artificial intelligence is developing algorithms that can generalize across multiple scenarios. To facilitate the evaluation of abstract reasoning capabilities, a comprehensive dataset known as the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) has been designed. ARC features 40 visually-oriented abductive reasoning tasks, divided into 80 stages consisting of 40 easy and 40 complex levels. To better understand how algorithms tackle abstract reasoning, we created the VisuAlGEn (VAG) dataset, containing 40 visual abduction tasks. We present a collection of 15 visual abductive reasoning tasks, further divided into 285 stages. We propose a range of baseline algorithms that can process ARC and VAG datasets. Additionally, we outline several research avenues for exploring more efficient artificial reasoning.

Motivated by contemporary research in fractional conservation laws, we investigate the characteristics of initial data for the nonlocal conservation law $u_t(x) + (\kappa(x)u^\alpha)_{x} = 0$, with a given bounded $\kappa$ and $\alpha > 0$. Within specific spaces of functions of bounded variation, we categorize the initial data for the nonlocal equation as being approximated by the corresponding data for the standard fractional conservation law $u_t + (Hu)_x = 0$, with a given fractional diffusion operator $H$.

Our research involves a detailed analysis of the $B_{s}^{0}$ to $D_{s}^{\mp} K^{\pm}$ decay using 3.0 fb$^{-1}$ of LHCb data collected during Run 1 and 1.9 fb$^{-1}$ of data from Run 2. We have discovered the branching fractions of these decays relative to others, with precise measurements revealing a ratio of approximately $0.332 \pm 0.040 \pm 0.015$ and $0.085 \pm 0.016 \pm 0.004$. These ratios are consistent with the Standard Model's predictions and do not indicate the presence of new physics.

In a distributed massive MIMO system, a significant increase in spectral efficiency can be achieved when both data transmission and channel feedback are simultaneously sent. However, a major challenge arises due to the severe co-channel interference between the data and channel feedback signals, which severely restricts the performance of the system. To address this issue, a novel transmission scheme is introduced, which involves a unique combination of two precoding matrices - one for data transmission and the other for channel feedback transmission. By employing a low-complexity semidefinite programming method, the scheme can achieve substantial improvements in spectral efficiency with minimal complexity. Simulation results demonstrate that this scheme can offer a significant gain in spectral efficiency over traditional methods while maintaining minimal complexity.

A novel privacy model has been developed using a cloud-based shuffle service within a local differential privacy framework. This new model differs from traditional local mechanisms by incorporating a post-processing step where data is shuffled and processed outside of users' control, leading to a cloud server's unknown location. Analytical studies demonstrate that our model provides stronger privacy protection, and with a modest increase in data upload, can achieve equivalent privacy compared to state-of-the-art private mechanisms.

This research paper presents an innovative coding technique called orthogonal time sequency multiplexing (OTSM), a breakthrough in orthogonal signal transmission that rivals the performance of orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). The authors delve into the theoretical underpinnings of OTSM, presenting a mathematical model for the transmission of a random sequence and deriving an analytical formula for the bit error rate (BER) in a noisy environment. Additionally, they introduce a sophisticated channel-adaptive modulation scheme called OTSM with adaptive power allocation (OTSMAPA), which dynamically adjusts transmission power across various communication channels. Extensive simulations using a Rayleigh fading model confirm that OTSMAPA surpasses the performance of its non-adaptive counterpart and other established signal processing methods, solidifying OTSM's potential as a cutting-edge transmission strategy.

Let's denote the weight on a semigroup $S$ as $\omega$. The $\ell^1$ algebra of $\omega$-weighted functions on $S$ is denoted by $L^1(\omega, S)$. The condition for $\omega$ to satisfy the F-property ($\mathcal F(S, \omega)$) means that for any $x, y$ in $S$, $\omega(xy)$ is less than or equal to $\omega(x) + \omega(y)$. This paper demonstrates that for weighted monoids or groups with the F-property, the unitalization of the semigroup is an $\ell^1$ space, thereby ensuring that the dual of $L^1(\omega, S)$ is contained in $L^1(\omega, U(S))$. Additionally, the conditions under which $L^1(\omega, S)$ is separable and $\ell^2(\omega, S)$ is complete are identified, particularly in the context of the $\mathcal A(S, \omega)$ condition which is more restrictive than the F-property. Furthermore, the $\ell^p$-boundedness of the Gelfand transform is established for $1 \leq p \leq 2$, and the dual of $L^1(\omega, S)$ is shown to be contained in $L^1(\omega, S^\ddag)$ under specific conditions.

The dynamic behavior of a molten metal melt pool under an intense laser beam is a complex phenomenon. The energy absorbed per unit area significantly influences the fluid flow patterns and laser-induced deformation in the melt pool. In the field of rapid prototyping, certain specific energy flux values are crucial for achieving desired melt pool behaviors. This study focuses on melt pool behavior at high energy flux levels, corresponding to laser intensities above 10^6 W/cm^2. The energy flux level is measured in a frame of reference moving with the melt pool, which is crucial for achieving an accurate energy flux and an accurate frame of reference. The laser beam is assumed to be thin and rectangular, and the melt pool is assumed to be a boundary layer melt pool. The energy flux through a given laser spot can be described by a Gaussian distribution in the laser beam's plane. The laser beam's plane is assumed to be two-dimensional, and the melt pool is assumed to be a boundary layer melt pool. The laser beam's plane is a critical parameter that needs to be considered. The energy flux's radial distribution can be described by a Gaussian distribution. The laser beam's power can be modeled as a Gaussian stochastic process, and the laser beam's spot can be modeled as a random variable. The laser beam's power is a time-dependent variable, and the laser beam's spot can be considered a fixed variable. The laser beam's power is a critical parameter that needs to be considered. In the future 6G network, public transportation vehicles are likely to incorporate cutting-edge wireless technology, including a vast array of connected devices and energy-recharging capabilities via a sophisticated radio interface. A key component of this vision involves the integration of radio energy harvesting technology into vehicle-to-vehicle communication systems. In this study, we propose an innovative, energy-neutral design for a communication system that utilizes vehicle-integrated radio energy harvesting and wireless charging technology in high-capacity public transportation vehicles. Specifically, vehicles equipped with wireless charging technology will not only recharge their batteries while in operation but also return to the starting point and dock for a full maintenance inspection. A novel vehicle-integrated radio energy harvesting and wireless charging technique is developed to ensure optimal energy efficiency, and we present a comprehensive analysis of the energy-neutral design, including mathematical formulas for an ideal vehicle-integrated system.

A key question in the study of Boolean functions, first answered by Alon, MOXER in 1986, posits the existence of an approximation polynomial of minimal degree that accurately approximates every Boolean function within a specific threshold. This inquiry is further explored in this paper, where we demonstrate the existence of infinitely many polynomials of varying degrees that accurately approximate every Boolean function within a specific threshold, but whose degree varies with the specific threshold, with degree requirements of $\sqrt{\log n}$ for a threshold of $1/2 - \varepsilon$ and $\sqrt{\log \log n}$ for a threshold of $1/2 + \varepsilon$.

Bistability is a common occurrence across various physical systems and plays a crucial part in understanding their intricate dynamics. While research has delved into the complex nature of bistability, a unified theoretical framework still lacks the depth and clarity it necessitates. This study proposes a novel unification theory for bistable systems, which offers a framework for the classification of two fundamental types of such structures. These fundamental types are characterized by distinct properties, such as the presence or absence of hysteresis, as well as different equilibrium paths, particularly in the form of saddle or half-steady state curves. These fundamental types can be distinguished by a characteristic curve, with a unique feature known as the unipotency condition. This condition is found to emerge from a specific transformation of the system's dynamics, particularly in terms of the gradient flow. This unipotency condition serves as a defining characteristic of the two fundamental types of bistability, providing a unified theoretical approach to understanding their complex dynamics.
This paper on spin polarized strange quark matter is focused on determining the thermodynamic properties of this state at finite temperature, using the MIT bag model.

This study delves into the realm of audio-visual correlation, exploring the underlying mechanisms that link sounds to visual representations. Our focus lies in the challenging task of generating high-quality features despite the scarcity of paired audio-visual data. To address this, we introduce a novel framework known as the dynamic feature and prototype alignment (DFPA) network. This network successfully leverages text-based descriptions to improve the performance of audio-visual correlation models. In a notable departure from previous approaches, DFPA optimizes audio and visual features for mutual alignment, thereby facilitating the exchange of information between the two modalities. To enhance its performance, DFPA incorporates a dynamic cross-modal matching strategy that effectively guides the alignment process. To better capture the intricate relationships between audio-visual features, we also propose a multi-branch strategy that utilizes both early and late fusion. Our experimental results demonstrate that DFPA outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in audio-visual correlation tasks, particularly in the challenging area of zero-shot audio-visual retrieval.

The Linear Ordering Problem involves determining all possible ways in which a set of n objects can be arranged in a sequence, where each object is connected to a specified number of others. This problem can be mathematically represented using a graph where each object is connected to its adjacent neighbors. The problem of finding all possible sequences, known as permutations, is known to be computationally difficult, requiring O(n!) operations for a brute-force solution. However, this paper presents a more efficient algorithm for arranging objects in a sequence, by approximating the sequence as the path that minimizes the number of large jumps in a graph representation. This method, called the Optimal Displacement Graph, is used to solve the problem, and its performance is compared with other heuristic methods.

The Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) phase transition occurs in superconductors when their dimension is significantly reduced, causing the destruction of long-range order due to vortex-antivortex unbinding. Researchers have attempted to replicate this phenomenon in topological insulators, specifically in the parafermion Ising model, at the edge of these one-dimensional structures. In this study, we investigate the interplay between BKT transitions and Majorana zero modes in a two-dimensional framework. We demonstrate that BKT transitions in the zero-mode sector can occur independently, yet influence each other due to their sector coupling. Furthermore, we identify a universal relationship between BKT transition temperatures and critical exponents.

Significant advancements in graph query languages have been made, primarily focusing on searching for paths within static graphs defined by edge connections. In contrast, temporal property graphs are dynamic and feature nodes and edges with attached time intervals, allowing for more complex path and time-dependent queries. To address this, we have developed an extension to the SQL language specifically tailored for temporal property graphs. Our query language, TPQL, goes beyond basic path queries, also supporting the specification of time constraints within these queries. Given the inherent complexity of processing temporal queries, we have created an optimized processing strategy for the results. Additionally, we have designed and implemented a query engine called Monsoon that leverages the TPQL language and operates on top of the Tiger graph database. Monsoon's results are promising, demonstrating substantial query performance gains of up to 6.3 times for path and time-dependent queries when compared to standard graph query languages.

The unique properties of ultracold atomic and molecular physics have led to a breakthrough in the field of chemical reactions. These unique properties allow for the examination of chemical phenomena under unexplored conditions, offering a new perspective on established theories. The application of ultracold physics has also enabled the development of innovative methods for controlling chemical reactions, which is particularly beneficial for the chemical industry. This review aims to provide an overview of the advancements in ultracold chemistry, focusing on recent discoveries, particularly in the fields of unbound and confined ultracold collisions, as well as the incorporation of optical control techniques.

We've developed a new timing method for the NEOWISE response to sudden solar system events, designed to analyze data within minutes. This approach allows for the immediate detection of transient phenomena like solar flares, lunar eclipses, and asteroid impacts, and the identification of thousands of previously hidden events, such as asteroid flashes, lunar meteoroid showers, and sudden changes in asteroid brightness caused by cometary activity or volcanic eruptions. This method, based solely on NEOWISE's fully available mid-infrared dataset, can process and analyze new events in real-time and is currently only limited by the rate at which WISE data is being released.

We investigate the ground state behavior of the spin-1/2 J1-J2 XY model in a square lattice within the dimer-dimer approximation. By examining phase diagrams for various values of J2/J1 and the ratio of ring exchange to Heisenberg exchange J3/J1, we find that the model's behavior is consistent with quantum dimer order. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the model's phase boundaries are largely unaffected by the value of J3/J1, except near the point of quantum criticality. By comparing our results to the density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) simulations, we find that the model's phases are consistent except at large values of J2/J1, where the model's boundaries deviate from those obtained through DMRG. Additionally, our results show that the model's critical point is consistent with existing quantum Monte Carlo simulations.

This study examines the impact of global events and domestic policies on international trade flows using a gravity equation framework.  Estimated results suggest that a significant portion of trade disruptions resulting from global events persists even after accounting for factors such as domestic policies. These persistent shocks are then grouped into two categories: persistent and non-persistent effects, which are identified through the use of panel heterogeneity and time effects.  The methodology allows researchers to assess the effects of changes in persistence, which is a relatively new area of study in trade modeling.  The results indicate that a significant proportion of trade disruptions resulting from global events are long-lasting, whereas those caused by domestic policies are relatively short-term.  This difference in long and short term persistence of shocks enables researchers to estimate the optimal trade policies that can mitigate negative effects of global events on trade flows.

A novel approach to construct exact solutions in four-dimensional noncommutative gauge theories is proposed. The method relies on introducing a supplementary, commutative coordinate and generalizing the Lagrangian to accommodate noncommutative coordinates. The solutions thus obtained can be translated into the noncommutative context by means of a commutation-based transformation. The solutions thus derived are valid and can be expressed in terms of the commutative coordinates. The solutions thus obtained are for noncommutative scalar fields, gauge fields, and gravity-like fields, including the associated field strengths and curvatures. The solutions are purely algebraic. The solutions thus obtained are valid and can be expressed in terms of commutative coordinates. The method also yields novel solutions for fields that lack commutative counterparts. The method's applicability is not restricted to specific field types or dimensions. The method's applicability is further explored for three-dimensional and five-dimensional noncommutative theories. The method's applicability is also extended to noncommutative theories with mixed or mixed-like geometry. The method's applicability is further extended to noncommutative theories with mixed or mixed-like geometry involving fields that transform under the Lorentz group.

To enhance quantum communication systems, coherent filtering can be applied by introducing a measure of coherence between a system and a reference state, allowing for faster recovery times in quantum evolution and thus preventing loss of information. Our proposal involves using coherent filtering in the development of a quantum repeater, enabling the efficient distribution of entangled states over multiple channels. Specifically, in two-dimensional Hilbert spaces, coherent filtering can be implemented with mirror symmetry, while in higher dimensions, it requires the use of unitary time-dependent interfaces. Our method involves designing these interfaces using a machine learning algorithm, which uses training data to optimize performance. Our results show that coherent filtering enables the distribution of entangled states with high fidelity, even with multiple channels, offering a novel approach to quantum repeaters.

The duration of time has long been an enigma for scientists. Research has shown that our internal mental state significantly influences how we perceive time's passage. This paper examines the psychological concept of time distortion and its effects on both individuals and society at large, including the potential to create artificial intelligence systems that process information faster or slowing down time relative to their environment. We will demonstrate the intricate relationship between time perception and mental state, and enable mental state control over time perception mechanics.

This research investigates how quickly and accurately professionals make decisions during a mentally demanding task by analyzing the relationship between speed and quality in professional chess. Utilizing data from 30 professional chess games, researchers found a positive correlation between the speed of decisions and their accuracy, which they attributed to the mental costs of processing information. To provide further insight into these costs, they broke down decision times into components such as preparation and reflection. The results showed that experienced players often prioritize efficiency over accuracy, making quicker decisions with comparable or superior quality compared to less experienced players.

To assess machine learning fairness, existing approaches rely on definitions derived from probabilistic theories rather than legal frameworks. This research examines the compatibility between existing definitions and concepts in U.S. anti-discrimination law by comparing the language of academic papers to court rulings. The analysis reveals a notable mismatch between mathematical definitions and legal principles, particularly with regards to the notion of 'protected characteristics'. The study identifies ideological disparities in four areas: the application of fairness across domains, the consideration of individual versus group characteristics, the emphasis on intended versus unintended outcomes, and the consideration of discrimination versus proportionality. The research concludes that some language in the machine learning fairness literature may be perceived as discriminatory or difficult to understand by non-experts.

The Atma nuclear decay experiment aims to identify tiny changes in electron and majoron neutrino masses within a controlled laboratory setting. By utilizing a large, optimized liquid argon target with advanced electronics, the Atma team plans to achieve better than a few sigma levels of precision within a short two-year time frame, which would significantly surpass previous research efforts. This project, which can be fully implemented at the short-baseline neutrino experiment SiteEVO's prototype facility, also has the potential to serve as a key validation experiment for the Argon Dark Photon project, which involves using ArTPC technology to detect dark matter.

This study explores the ground state properties of $\Lambda$-nucleon and $\Lambda$-neutron nuclei, such as $p$-wave separation energies and density distributions, using two distinct types of chiral baryon-baryon interactions within the context of the Faddeev calculations. Variations in the meson exchange patterns of the BB interactions significantly impact $p$-wave separation energies, and their differences can be leveraged to investigate density profiles of the nuclei. Additionally, this research examines the relationship between density and $p$-wave separation energy, and it's found that the former linearly increases with the latter, enabling the exploration of novel constraints on the density profiles.

This paper outlines a straightforward, low-tech approach for attaining Facebook\textcircled{1} privacy, which offers a striking balance between user-friendly access and robust privacy protection, making it more appealing to the majority of users who may not be interested in fully severing their online and offline lives.

Consider a simple branching random walk in d-dimensional space, denoted as BRW, and a Poisson point process of random environments, denoted as E, with a mean Poisson measure. Let the random interlude process, D, be defined as the random distance between successive branching random walkers in a general state under the influence of E. By conditioning on the environments, D is transformed into a coalescent point process, denoted as Q, with a characteristic property of a mixture of a Poisson process and a gamma process. This coalescent point process, D conditioned on E, represents a type of non-linear clock process. Our study focuses on the random environments, D conditioned on BRW, which is equivalent to a mixed Poisson process with a mixed renewal process. This representation enables us to derive the conditional Laplace transform of the random environments, which is a key tool for analyzing the random environments, D.

We examine a hard core model on the Cayley tree, specified by parameters that define the statistical system. We identify the conditions necessary for a periodic Gibbs measure to exist, and under these conditions, we find that a family of such measures comprising periodic hypercycles is unique. Additionally, our analysis shows that the periodic hypercycle measures coincide across all translation classes if and only if the specified parameters define a model that's either trivial or contains a singularity with a rational index.

The LAMOST survey, a large-scale astronomical observation project, covers a vast area of the Milky Way and its surroundings. It systematically collects detailed information about the movement, composition, and properties of stars and galaxies in the region, including precise distances and chemical makeup. The survey's data, particularly its spectroscopic results, offers valuable insights into various astrophysical phenomena, including the evolution of galaxies and the formation of stars. The LAMOST survey relies on a significant network of 480-500 telescopes spread across nearly 60 locations in China, supported by 20-30 collaborators.

To determine the isotope shift of the $5d^9 6f^1~^3D^1$J = 1 state in Sr, we conducted an absolute isotope shift measurement using a lamp emitting on the $5d~^1D_{1}$ state and a high-resolution Fourier transform interferometer at the FEL-Jeans Laboratory. The obtained results for the $5d^9~6f^1~^3D^1$ state in Sr and the $5d^9~6f^1~^3D^1$ and $5d^9~7f^1~^3F^1$ states in SrX (where X = Ca, Zr, Sn), were used to calculate the nuclear charge radii of Sr and the SrX isotopes. The measured values of the isotope shift of the $5d^9~7f^1~^3F^1$ state in SrX were found to be consistent with the nuclear charge radii derived from the SRAM model and recent atomic data. The results of the atomic data are also consistent with the calculated nuclear charge radii of the SrX isotopes obtained from the SRAM model and the measured nuclear charge radii of the SrX isotopes obtained from the TRIGATI technique.

In the field of quantum information theory, specific states of quantum systems are called graph states. These states are characterized by a specific property known as the complementarity principle. This principle can be described as a visual representation where the system's measurements on a graph show connected measurements canceling each other out. This paper proposes an algorithm to mathematically generate graph states using a method called the perfect matching formula.

Hall's Theorem provides a foundational result in the realm of set systems, specifying that given a set of n sets, each containing at least n/U elements, there exists U transversal elements within the collections. This primitive statement has been a cornerstone for developing numerous important algorithms and set system characteristics in the realm of combinatorial mathematics. To date, Hall's Theorem remains the only known non-trivial decision algorithm for finding a transversal within a subset collection of a matroid, where the transversal's cardinality is unknown. To address this, the current work presents an efficient method for identifying a nearly global transversal within a matroid, where the method leverages a matroid's independent subsets and their respective cardinalities. Notably, the proposed algorithm demonstrates an improved time complexity, specifically being linear in the number of elements within the matroid, when the U value is a polynomial function of 1/b.

This research examines the most efficient method for selecting cloud video virtual machines to optimize the video rendering experience, while also considering the virtual machine's availability. The study centers on video transcoding as a sample task, evaluating the video virtual machine's performance in terms of processing speed, storage capacity, and availability status. The study's key contribution lies in developing an algorithm that identifies the most suitable cloud video virtual machine for the video transcoding task based on available performance metrics.
