This research utilizes a combination of the Taylor-Peach-Richard continuum dislocation theory and a strain rate approach to establish a unified constitutive model that accurately predicts the plasticity of a $\text{Ti-6Al}$ alloy, which has undergone cold-rolling, under various conditions. The developed model can be applied to a wide range of rolling orientations and temperatures, yielding a strong correlation with experimental data. Specifically, the model's predictions for the critical shear stress and strain are heavily influenced by the concentration of $\text{Ti}(\text{C})$ inclusions and grain orientation, respectively. Furthermore, this model can be used to establish a correlation between the yield or flow stress and strain, which remains consistent across different temperatures and rolling orientations, effectively providing a single, unified relationship that encompasses all scenarios.

Software product lines consist of interrelated systems with unique sets of features.
Feature models are the standard tool for modeling the variability of software product lines, outlining features and their relationships.
Feature models contain elements called features and relationships between features, which can be described using Graph Theory to analyze their structure.
Feature selection is a critical process in software data mining that involves choosing relevant features from a set of features.
Our research aims to develop an innovative feature selection technique specifically designed for software feature models based on the complexity of their structure.
This new technique utilizes features and relationships from feature models as input to select relevant features and reduce the complexity of software systems.

A newly developed software module named KSPF is designed for post-processing data from cameras with monolithic arrays, particularly those with a square pixel array. This module is capable of producing science frames with reduced pixel size and enhanced image quality. KSPF is primarily created for use with the K2 mission's CCDs, but it can also be adapted for analysis of other data. In this study, we apply KSPF to the analysis of data from the mission's short period and long cadence observations. We also utilize KSPF to produce reduced images of specific fields observed by the K2 mission. In doing so, we identify previously unseen faint companions around stars. Our results show that the method is highly effective, achieving a high level of image quality within specific requirements. We also demonstrate the method's effectiveness on full frame images of specific fields observed by the K2 mission. In doing so, we produce high quality images that are comparable to the original data. Our analysis reveals the presence of previously identified astrometric binaries and faint companions that were not visible in the original data. We also show that the method can be adapted for analysis of data from other missions, such as the Kepler mission. In doing so, we produce high quality images that are comparable to the original data.

We examine the thermodynamic and energetic characteristics of the Vaidya outgoing flux produced during a black hole's gradual evaporation process. To calculate the associated symmetries, we draw on the entropy of the Hawking radiation as a reference standard. Furthermore, we use entropy-splitting techniques to derive flux-specific entropy levels, then apply these to model a black hole's gradual evaporation. This process is used to determine the impact of the flux-specific entropies on the thermodynamic and energetic characteristics of the evaporation. Lastly, we explore the role of the flux-specific entropies in the black hole's eventual disappearance.

In Weyl semimetals, Fermi arcs are connective regions between Weyl branches in the surface Brillouin zone. Our study focuses on Fermi arcs in the presence of spin-orbit coupling and an external magnetic field. We demonstrate that applying the Floquet formalism to a two-dimensional model with time-varying mass results in Fermi arcs with a corkscrew structure. At specific points, these arcs transform into closed loops, which persist as long as the material remains a Weyl semimetal.

Recent breakthroughs in video prediction have largely been driven by the introduction of novel training methods that rely on the dynamics of a sequence, rather than relying on the characteristics of the content. This approach has led to the development of several reinforcement learning training objectives that can effectively model these dynamics, resulting in highly accurate predictions. However, training these models is challenging, particularly when conducted in a self-supervised manner, which often requires vast amounts of data. This difficulty has prompted the creation of more efficient training methods, such as the use of virtual ground truth, which has shown promise in significantly reducing the required amount of data. This study presents a new virtual ground truth training method that builds upon the spatial transformer module, which has shown effectiveness in handling the complexities of video data. By leveraging this module, our approach effectively models the dynamics of a video sequence and achieves the highest accuracy in predicting multiple frames, particularly when compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

Mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) are linked to severe diseases and aging processes.
A new method for identifying these mutations is needed, as existing techniques are time-consuming and limited in scope.
This study introduces a novel approach to detecting mitochondrial DNA mutations using machine learning and NGS data, utilizing primers from 13 different regions across the mitochondrial genome.
This method has several key features: it uses a combination of positional and probabilistic machine learning models, allows for the selection of specific regions of interest, and provides an identification score that corresponds to the likelihood of a mutation in each region.
Our model performed well when tested on a subset of a public mitochondrial mutation dataset, demonstrating an average precision of 0.75 and recall of 0.83 at a threshold of 0.05.
Furthermore, when applied to a comprehensive dataset of human aging, our model was able to accurately differentiate between healthy 20-year-olds and 80-year-olds using the same data, producing an accuracy of 0.85 and an improvement of 0.04 compared to a baseline model.
This study highlights the potential of machine learning models to detect mitochondrial DNA mutations and identify signs of aging in humans.

This study introduces a non-autoregressive speech model that generates mel-spectrograms for any given duration.
To achieve this, we develop a cutout distribution that models the mel-spectrograms of a speech sample by dividing it into fixed-length segments.
We then use a neural network to determine the optimal positions for these segments.
The proposed model optimizes both the spectral content and temporal alignment of speech samples in one go.
Experimental results show that this approach surpasses existing models in both quality and efficiency when the neural network is able to determine all segment positions accurately.

The ternary alloy, Ge-Sb-Te, is a crucial component in optical and magneto-optical devices such as optical disks and optical filters. To study the alloy's behavior, researchers have conducted in-depth research on Ge-Sb-Te films, focusing on their structural, electrical, and optical properties. The research involved analyzing the alloy's phase transitions, electrical conductivity, and optical characteristics in Ge-Sb-Te films, and the results were compared to those of the binary Ge-Sb and Sb-Te alloys. The findings indicate that the alloy's phase transitions occur through a process of phase separation, and the phase stability is influenced by the stoichiometry of the alloy. The results also show that the alloy's behavior can be explained by the competition between the formation of Ge-Te and Sb-Te clusters.

We introduce a novel, exactly solvable model of a Kitaev chain on a 3D lattice that supports the emergence of fractional topological phases. This model is grounded in a dual interpretation of the 3D lattice as a 1D chain with periodic time. By leveraging the Hamiltonian's time periodicity, we demonstrate the existence of phases where Majorana edge modes accumulate a quantized phase of π over the lattice period, yielding a topological insulator phase. This phase is characterized by the presence of a protected π-flux, a novel phenomenon that gives rise to additional topological insulator phases, including one with a non-Abelian symmetry and two antichiral counterparts.

The thermal structure of a protoplanetary disc, particularly around forming planets, is influenced by dust traps and cavities. We have developed a model to simulate the thermal and chemical behavior of a disc, taking into account the formation of gaps created by a protoplanet. We have found that the temperature within these gaps is lower than the surrounding areas, with the difference in temperature between the gaps and halos increasing with the disc's radius. We have also observed that the disc's surface density in the gap region is reduced, leading to a decrease in midplane temperature. Our model suggests that the disc's cooling rate, particularly in the gap region, is influenced by the amount of gas within these cavities, taking longer when the gaps are larger.

When working with high-dimensional observations in reinforcement learning, creating new data through minimal alterations can be challenging due to the need for new features that can be learned by the agent. To address this challenge, we've developed a new approach called the Induced Transition Operator (ITO). The ITO method uses a separate, smaller network to generate a latent representation of an environment's state, allowing for the creation of artificial transitions that can be used to augment the training data. This technique can be applied to various environments and has several benefits, including the ability to control the type of information the agent uses to make decisions, as well as the ability to focus on specific tasks within those environments. In our experiments, the ITO method outperformed existing approaches in a range of tests on environments with varying levels of complexity.

With approximately 300 million native speakers, Arabic ranks among the five most widely spoken languages globally, with the majority living within the Arab region.  Although modern standard Arabic is the official language of the Arab countries, there exist numerous dialects spoken by local populations, making dialect processing a pressing concern.  This paper provides an in-depth examination of the current state of the field, commencing with an overview of available Arabic dialect identification methods and datasets, followed by the presentation of various PID schemes, followed by an evaluation of the current state of PDI systems on well-known benchmarks.  Ultimately, this paper offers a summary of the study's key findings along with proposed future research avenues in this area of interest.

The Strip Packing problem involves arranging n rectangles, called items, into a fixed-length, continuous strip of width. The goal is to minimize waste and fill the strip to maximum capacity. This problem variant, called the Guillotine Strip Packing problem, has the added constraint that strips and pieces can be divided into smaller pieces using straight cuts only. To address this issue, we developed a new search-based algorithm called StripCut. This algorithm uses a modified version of the vertex representation, paired with a novel move exploration strategy, to find a solution. Moreover, we also developed a new evaluation function aimed at identifying the most promising moves. The StripCut algorithm significantly outperforms existing algorithms for this problem variant, improving solution quality and finding solutions much quicker.

A novel approach is introduced to accurately infer the mass of galaxy clusters from high-resolution X-ray maps, by applying a deep generative model that uses information about the cluster's mass distribution, projected density, and associated X-ray signals. This approach involves training a neural network to generate a 3D density map from a constrained set of 2D projections, and then using an ensemble of these networks to calculate the mass distribution's peak and associated properties. Our method is validated using mock galaxy cluster simulations that mimic the characteristics of upcoming X-ray surveys, and we demonstrate that it can accurately infer the mass of galaxy clusters with a precision of 10%. Furthermore, combining our results with information on cluster redshifts, yields an accurate mass estimate with a precision of 5%. This method is also shown to be resilient to the presence of interloper clusters and background noise.

Traditionally, LDA and MMDP models rely on word boundaries to segment text, but many languages lack explicit segmentation. To address this, tokenization methods using Pearson's chi-squared test and t-statistics are employed to determine optimal token boundaries.

The rapid discovery of numerous pulsar candidates through machine learning is hampered by the issue of class imbalance, which severely hinders validation and follow-up investigations. This problem is amplified in the context of the pulsar timing array project's candidate pool, comprised of hundreds of thousands of radio frequency interference-like signals, most of which do not represent pulsars. This study introduces a novel approach to address the class imbalance issue, using the established classification model as the foundation and focusing on mitigating its impact on the model's generalization capabilities. The proposed method, which involves re-sampling the minority class (pulsars) to balance data, is then applied to the candidate selection task. The method's efficacy is demonstrated using the AI-driven candidate identification system for the Parkes Fast Radio Burst search, which accurately detected 12 pulsars out of 334,000 candidates. The method's performance is further validated through the evaluation of precision, recall, and the area under the curve for the receiver operating characteristic, yielding notable improvements. Consequently, this approach enables the reduction of false positives while maintaining true positives, thereby facilitating efficient follow-up investigations.

Given a $\sigma$-finite measure space $(X,\mu)$ and a group $G$, consider the full crossed product $C^*$-algebra associated with a $W^*$-algebra $A$ and the measure space $X$ equipped with a Fell bundle. When $G$ is an amenably acting group on $(X,\mu)$, it follows that the Fell bundle has a bounded approximate identity. Furthermore, under the condition of $G$ being a compactly acting group on $(X,\mu)$ and $A$ being a simple $\sigma$-unital $W^*$-algebra, we show that the associated Fell bundle has a bounded trace. These conclusions are illustrated by applying them to several instances of weighted shifts acting on the Lebesgue measure space over a countable infinite set.

The prolate spheroidal wave functions have been widely used in various fields, 
such as signal processing, electromagnetic theory, quantum mechanics and the like. 
In this paper, we derive a closed-form formula for the normalized prolate spheroidal wave function with integer order and establish its asymptotic form. These findings not only provide a straightforward derivation but also supplement existing literature with the added benefit of compactness.

We introduce a machine-learning approach to remove background noise from electron
micrographs of 3D crystals, which are challenging to separate from the crystal
structure. Our proposed method employs a score function derived from a specific type of
crystal image called a unit cell, which is trained using a set of high-quality crystal
images. Unlike existing techniques, our approach learns the noise characteristics of
crystal images without relying on a noise model. Furthermore, our method can be
applied to any type of crystal image without prior knowledge of the crystal structure.
Our results indicate that the denoising process enhances the quality of the crystal
image without compromising the crystal's essential features. Notably, this method
can be used for a wide range of crystal images, including those from crystals with
unknown structures.

The Lagrangian approach in ocean studies tracks water flow by following specific particles, identifying areas where these particles congregate can reveal where the ocean is mixing with itself, where oceanic eddies are forming and breaking, and where large-scale circulation patterns are present. This report showcases the capabilities of the tool, lizo, which applies the Lagrangian approach to satellite data to study oceanic motion in various regions, such as the polar seas, the Gulf Stream, and the Indian Ocean eddy activity.

Our investigation of the thermodynamic scaling principle during the glass formation process utilizes a rigorous method to calculate specific heat and configurational entropy density. Through a detailed analysis of a two-dimensional Lennard-Jones system, we demonstrate that a particular thermodynamic scaling emerges when the temperature is measured relative to a specific time and length scale. This relative temperature is directly linked to the dynamic threshold determined from the free particle dynamics. We demonstrate that this threshold corresponds to a temperature at which a specific heat anomaly appears, reflecting the onset of non-standard thermodynamic behavior. This temperature is found to be identical to a critical temperature associated with the glass formation process. Furthermore, we show that a particular thermodynamic scaling is a natural consequence of a specific type of glass dynamics. This is illustrated through a general model of a glass that exhibits dynamic behavior consistent with the observed principle.

This paper explores the semi-discrete analogue of the $\overline{\rm SH}$-transformed modified Camassa-Holm equation. Initially, we establish the semi-discrete $\overline{\rm SH}$-transform for semi-discrete mCH equations and identify its inherent integrability characteristics. Subsequently, we derive semi-discrete forms of four integrable bi-Hamiltonian systems associated with the semi-discrete mCH equation. Ultimately, through Lie symmetry reduction, we derive two essential integrable systems linked to the semi-discrete mCH equation and show that these systems correspond to semi-discrete versions of the Camassa-Holm and Novikov equations.

Quantum mechanics has been found to accurately model various physical systems, yet it contradicts traditional understanding of causality and free will. Systems governed by Schrodinger's equation are said to be non-contextual, yet this assumption is being reevaluated. Our research suggests redefining quantum state variables to the wave functions, which are fundamental to the contextuality of quantum systems, thus allowing for a causal and deterministic alternative to the wave function without compromising its predictive power.

We have conducted an in-depth analysis of the orbital dynamics in various compact binary systems featuring gravitational interactions between a black hole and neutron star, as well as between two neutron stars. Our work involves solving the spin dynamics of these binary systems to the third post-Newtonian order, and we have found that our results match the established equations of motion accurately up to the tenth order of post-Newtonian accuracy when accounting for the highest order of spin-spin interactions. Our work provides a detailed understanding of the orbital dynamics of these binary systems, which can be applied to various post-Newtonian waveforms and potentially to the study of gravitational waves produced by these binary systems.

This work presents the "You Only Look Once" (YOLO) object detection method as equivalent to a single neural network stage, thereby eliminating the need for a traditional two-stage approach to object detection. By integrating all prediction processes into a single input layer, a fully convolutional architecture, YOLO dispenses with the need to generate proposed regions of interest. Furthermore, the proposed method utilizes an image's total area to estimate the number of objects within an input frame, thereby estimating the output size required for object classification. The proposed method optimizes the output size by adjusting the image's scaling factor, which is determined by the network's input size. The proposed method is evaluated using the PASCAL VOC 2007 and PASCAL VOC 2012 datasets, resulting in average precision scores of 0.8578 and 0.7644, respectively, for the class of all objects.

We examine a substantial quote database containing over 67,000 quotes from more than 6,700 distinct job titles spanning 131 countries. The initial investigation reveals that in a large quote dataset extracted from Wikipedia, job titles and affiliations are inaccurately represented. Specifically, we discovered that countries of origin are often misrepresented, with either overcounting or undercounting prevalent. Affiliations within the dataset are also marred by inaccuracies, with either overrepresentation or underrepresentation prevalent. Furthermore, a substantial proportion of quotes are linked to missing affiliations. To rectify these issues, we propose a method for inferring missing affiliations based on job titles, grounded in the concept of distributional semantic meaning. This approach leverages a large corpus of English text data, comprising 400GB of content, to develop a dictionary mapping job titles to countries, thereby facilitating the correction of inaccurately attributed quotes.

Decision trees and their ensembles have proven to be highly effective in supervised machine learning, primarily due to their interpretability and ability to handle both categorical and numerical features. However, their performance is heavily dependent on determining the optimal split values at each split point. Current approaches, such as the standard CART and LightGBM trees, often select split points that maximize classification criteria along the split line, a strategy which has been found to be suboptimal in previous research. In response, a new learning-by-bootstrapping algorithm is introduced that selects split points which maximize classification power while minimizing uncertainty. This approach is shown to be particularly effective in classification tasks and results in more robust ensemble classification trees with superior performance, which has been demonstrated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

The machine learning ecosystem is shaped by the interplay of various components such as models, data, and software, and its evaluation should consider multiple criteria in order to steer future developments toward specific applications. This paper introduces ML Ecosystem Evaluation, a framework that supports the decision-making process in choosing a particular machine learning model or feature within a given ecosystem. It also discusses the challenges of implementing this framework and presents some possible solutions.

In real-world applications, data often arrives in a stream and has unknown patterns, making it challenging to train models effectively. Current approaches using online clustering methods struggle to recognize and classify rare data classes, making it difficult to understand these data's underlying characteristics. To address this issue, we propose an online clustering method called COCO (Cognitive Online Clustering) that leverages knowledge graphs to discover data patterns. By incorporating various existing online clustering techniques, we enhance their performance using knowledge graph reasoning. Our approach enables the identification of rare data classes and provides insights into their semantic meanings, achieving this through knowledge graph completion and reasoning. Our experimental results demonstrate that COCO outperforms existing online clustering methods, especially when dealing with rare data classes, and provides meaningful semantic interpretations of the clustered data.

In materials science and life sciences, coherent diffraction imaging techniques face significant challenges when dealing with strongly scattering samples. We have found a solution to this problem in ptychography, which combines focused beams with rotational and translational scanning to produce high-resolution images. Despite its potential, ptychographic reconstruction is often computationally complex. To address this, we have developed a new, more efficient method based on the Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm. By incorporating prior knowledge, our approach allows for faster convergence and more precise results. It can be applied in both inverse scattering and phase retrieval, and is particularly useful in ptychographic x-ray imaging for images with high speckle noise.

This paper develops a framework for probability distributions of time-dependent macroscopic properties for open systems under fluctuating environmental conditions. It demonstrates that the gauge invariance property allows for the derivation of these distribution probabilities in relation to the thermodynamic cost of the observable. Key to our approach is the identification of a fundamental Hamiltonian that underlies thermodynamic transformations. Our method involves solving the Schrödinger equation with time-dependent boundary conditions in order to derive the Schrödinger operators for the system and its environment. This formalism is then applied to commonly encountered operators such as the activity of binding events and the thermodynamic free energy, resulting in well-known expressions. Additionally, we show that the proposed formalism can be used to derive the Fokker-Planck equation governing fluctuations in the system's thermodynamic cost, and we establish a relationship between the stationary solution of the Fokker-Planck equation and the cumulant-generating function of the observable.

Neural networks have proven effective in solving complex problems through training and being applied to data sets, but a separate method called reservoir computing uses a pre-defined neural framework and maps new data into it. Studies have shown that this method can be effective even with just a few neurons. The following research explores the properties of a reservoir computing unit that utilizes a random and unstructured network, and it finds that its effectiveness depends heavily on its design characteristics. The following factors were found to influence its performance: its internal complexity, the strength of its internal connections, and the type of non-linear function used to process data. The study used a variety of input data sources including random, natural speech, and time-series data, and it found that a simple non-linear function performed best, even surpassing more complex neural methods in some cases. The study also found that a unit with a higher number of internal connections performed better than one with fewer connections, and that a critical threshold may exist beyond which performance improves rapidly.

We investigate the dynamics of a three-boson system confined within a weakly attractive potential, with one of its parameters suddenly altered. The system's behavior is significantly influenced by Efimov states, which cause periodic fluctuations in the particle density and substantial oscillations in the three-particle correlation. Notably, these correlations exhibit larger amplitudes than the one-particle correlation, and they persist for much longer periods. Our research suggests that these characteristics, particularly the extensive periods of oscillation, can be attributed to the system's three-body Efimov states, even when only a single Efimov state is significantly affected by the quench.

This research explores the field of quantum machine learning (QML) and its applications in quantum computing systems.  We examine quantum machine learning algorithms, specifically quantum kernel methods, and discuss implementations using quantum circuits.  We demonstrate a quantum machine learning system built with Google's quantum hardware and report the results of our experiments.  We find that the project's outcomes are in line with the quantum random model and reflect real-world computational times.  We also discuss potential quantum computing system improvements to enhance QML and quantum data analysis.

We introduce a new class of numerical quadrature formulas designed for approximating continuous integrals of vector fields over a two-dimensional area. This methodology relies on integrating Green's identities, particularly a modified version of the third identity as adapted by Phillips and Harrison. This approach enables efficient computation of Newtonian potentials across intricate domains through a detailed analysis of the potential's derivative on the boundary of these areas. We have developed a precise error assessment and a streamlined implementation, exemplified through various applications, including solving the incompressible Euler equations and the time-dependent Poisson equation.
